title: Nashik Is Spending ₹25,000 Crore to Rebuild Itself Before the Kumbh. Here's What NRIs Need to Know
excerpt: With the 2027 Simhastha Kumbh Mela barely a year away, Maharashtra is tearing up ghats, laying ring roads, and deploying AI crowd management — transforming one of Hinduism's holiest cities into something its diaspora may barely recognise
body:
The last time Nashik hosted the Simhastha Kumbh Mela, in 2015, an estimated three crore pilgrims descended on a city whose infrastructure groaned under the weight. Narrow lanes around the Godavari's sacred ghats became impassable. Sanitation was improvised. The experience, for many returning NRIs who had flown halfway around the world for a holy dip, oscillated between transcendence and logistical chaos.

Maharashtra has decided that will not happen again.

## A City Under Construction

The numbers are staggering. The central and state governments have committed a combined ₹25,000 crore to transform Nashik ahead of the Kumbh Mela that begins in July 2027 and runs through February 2028. Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis has personally set deadlines, and the scale of work underway is visible from satellite imagery.

The centrepiece is the **Nashik Parikrama**, a ₹3,659-crore ring road designed to absorb the estimated five crore visitors expected this time. The project, cleared by the state government, aims for completion by March 2027 — cutting it close, but reflecting the political urgency behind the effort.

The **Ministry of Railways** has committed ₹393 crore to expand Nashik's rail infrastructure, including platform extensions, signalling upgrades, and enhanced connectivity to handle pilgrim surges. The Nashik Municipal Corporation has separately requested ₹120 crore specifically for repairing the ageing bathing ghats along the Godavari — the very spots where millions will take their sacred dip.

## Ghats Razed and Rebuilt

The most visible transformation is at **Ramkund**, the holiest stretch of the Godavari in Nashik. The northern Ramkund area has been closed for two months as the iconic landmark building — historically used as a women's changing room — is demolished under the Ram Kal Path redevelopment project. Twelve new ghats are being constructed across Nashik and Trimbakeshwar to spread pilgrim density and improve safety.

For NRIs who last visited Nashik's ghats as children, carried on a parent's shoulders through a crushing crowd, the physical landscape of their memory is being systematically replaced. The new infrastructure promises to be safer, wider, and better serviced — but the narrow, ancient feel of the old ghats will be gone.

## AI Meets Ancient Ritual

What distinguishes this Kumbh from every previous edition is technology. CM Fadnavis has mandated AI-driven crowd management systems, digital publicity initiatives, and what officials describe as "the most technology-enabled Kumbh Mela in history." The state's 4,500-bus fleet from MSRTC will be deployed with a dedicated Kumbh Mela transport authority overseeing operations.

Riverbed sanitation — historically one of the most challenging aspects of any Kumbh — is receiving dedicated attention, with modern sewage systems being installed along the Godavari's banks. For diaspora visitors accustomed to questioning the water quality their parents bathed in without a second thought, this is a meaningful upgrade.

## Holy Dates and Planning

The **Simhastha Kumbh Mela 2027** holy bath dates run from July 2027 to February 2028, concluding on February 20, 2028. The key shahi snaan dates — the most auspicious bathing days that draw the largest crowds — will be announced closer to the event based on planetary alignments.

NRIs planning to attend should note that the construction timeline means visiting Nashik before March 2027 will involve navigating an active construction zone. Hotels and dharamshalas in the Panchavati area are already fielding advance bookings. Flights into Nashik's Ozar Airport and Pune (three hours by road) are the primary air routes.

## More Than Infrastructure

For all the concrete and steel, the Kumbh remains what it has always been — the world's largest act of collective faith. The Godavari at Nashik holds a particular significance in Hindu cosmology: it is here that Rama is believed to have performed last rites for his father Dasharatha during his exile, making every dip an act of ancestral remembrance.

The ₹25,000-crore investment is not merely about managing crowds. It is India signalling that its civilisational heritage deserves world-class infrastructure — the same instinct that drove the Kashi Vishwanath Corridor and the Ram Mandir. For NRIs who have felt the pull of a Kumbh but hesitated at the logistics, Nashik 2027 may be the one where modern India finally meets the ancient pilgrimage halfway.
